Subject: Galileo dedicated capacity: tokens/sec model and SLA buffer

Alex — thanks again for the time today. Per our conversation, I sketched a first-pass dedicated-capacity sizing model so we can align on the SLA targets and the commit required to cover steady-state + burst windows. Can you confirm the traffic profile (attached) is representative for Q3? A few asks up front: 

- Confirm target SLO: p95 end-to-end completion latency <= 450ms for 128-token completions (this is what we used below).
- Confirm % of calls that are short completions (<64 tokens) vs long (>256 tokens) — I used 60/40 split.
- Any regulatory constraints on model residency (US-only) or private VPC preferred?

Attached: galileo_demand_profile.csv (you mentioned you would send a cleaned export); I included a rough worksheet but haven't tuned kernel selection or quantization knobs.

Quick notes on methodology (high-level):
- Baseline throughput per 80GB A100-equivalent slot (optimized kernels, int8-ish quant) = 1,800 tokens/sec for the average request shape used here (128 token completion, 8 prefix tokens). This is our measured median for the model class you indicated.
- Autoscale warmup and steady-state assumptions: we model a dedicated slab (reserved) sized to cover 95% of minute-level demand and a burst pool (shared capacity) sized to absorb short spikes.
- Safety buffer / headroom: we recommend 25% operational buffer over 95% demand to cover queueing jitter, kernel warmups, and degraded performance during rolling upgrades.

I'll convert this into a one-page summary with explicit GPU counts and projected monthly token units if the attached CSV is the final demand shape.

Next step: if the attached demand sheet looks right, I'll send a recommended slab diagram (how many reserved GPUs, burst pool size, fallback model mapping) for your procurement and infra review.

Thanks — Naomi

Alex — got the CSV, thanks. I ran the worksheet and encoded a few configuration choices; summary below. Quoted the specific lines from the worksheet so procurement has the numbers they can act on.

Summary (baseline + burst sizing) — assumptions: p95 latency target 450ms, request mix 58/30/12 short/mid/long, average completion length 128 tokens, reserved hw = A100-80GB class perf = 1,800 tok/s per GPU (int8-like runtime).

1) Steady-state (95% minute-level demand):
- 95% minute-level tokens/sec demand observed in CSV = 4,200 tokens/sec.
- GPUs needed (reserve) = ceil(4,200 / 1,800) = 3 GPUs.
- Add 25% operational buffer → 3 * 1.25 = 3.75 → round up to 4 reserved GPUs.

2) Burst handling (95->99.9% short spikes):
- 99.9% minute-level peak = 21,600 tokens/sec (short spikes during biz hours).
- Additional GPUs to cover peak without queueing = ceil((21,600 - 4,200) / 1,800) = ceil(17,400 / 1,800) = 10 GPUs (burst pool).
- Recommendation: 4 reserved GPUs + 10 burst-capable GPUs = 14 GPUs total during peak windows.

3) Fallback and graceful degradation mapping:
- Primary model (70B, quantized) on reserved slab for best quality (p95 target).
- Fallback to 13B quantized variant for burst overflow — 13B runs ~2.8x tokens/sec on same hardware (approx 5,000 tok/s per GPU). When we hit 90% of burst pool, route non-critical traffic to 13B and reduce tokens consumed on 70B.

4) Ops & rollout notes:
- Warm cache strategy: pre-warm KV cache for top 20 prompts to reduce cold-start churn during morning spikes.
- Canary plan: start with 2 reserved GPUs committed for negotiated 3-month pilot; if telemetry matches projection, expand reserved to full 4 GPUs. The burst pool can be used pay-as-you-go while procurement finalizes a longer commit.

Monthly units and rough cost signals (ballpark for procurement conversation):
- Monthly tokens (projected steady) ~ 4,200 tok/s * 3600 * 24 * 30 ≈ 10.9B tokens/month (this is steady-state window only; bursts add variable tokens).
- GPU-hours reserved (4 GPUs) = 4 * 24 * 30 = 2,880 GPU-hours/month. Burst pool is metered.

Attachments: redwood_proposed_slab_diagram.pdf (slab + routing map), I also pushed the detailed workbook to the Drive link in the HubSpot note.

If you want, I can convert the math above into a procurement-ready line-item quote (commit tiers: 3mo pilot, 12mo discounted commit, optional burst cap). Tell me which commit tiers procurement prefers and I’ll format the quote.

Thanks — Naomi

Looping in ops and delivery notes — couple of practical changes from an engineering/deployment standpoint: 

- Replace "A100-80GB class" language with explicit SKU choices in the quote: we recommend reserved on 1x8 L40s for cost-efficiency but can map to A100-80GB if customer requires it. L40 perf baseline we used in later bench runs: ~1,650 tok/s for the 70B quantized baseline (I flagged that variance in the Drive workbook). Procurement should see both SKU pricing lines.
- Proposed SLA commitment tiers to include: 3-month pilot (no discount), 12-month commit (12% discount), 24-month commit (20% discount + guaranteed burst slab hold).
- Ops ask: Add a 15-minute pre-warm runbook to the onboarding checklist; this reduces p95 by ~60-80ms for typical prompt set (observed in previous customer pilots).

Action items: 
1) Naomi — can you produce a procurement-ready line-item that includes both L40 and A100 SKU rows, burst pool metered pricing, and the fallback routing clause? (We should keep the pricing band clear for procurement to compare).
2) Marissa — can you prepare an ops onboarding checklist (pre-warm steps, canary traffic % by hour, rolling-update guardrails) and attach to the quote package?
3) Karthik — please add a quick note on quantization sensitivity (quality delta) between 70B int8 and 13B int8 fallback so procurement knows the quality tradeoffs.

Alex — copying you; procurement wants the two-SKU comparison and a clear pilot path before legal signs any commit.
